learning_outcomes.text: Students will know the characteristics and behaviors of deformable solids.
Students will understand and apply the concepts of Elasticity and Strength of Materials to solve for displacements, deformations, and stresses in real solids.
Students will learn to size and calculate the mechanical resistance, stiffness, and stability of resistant elements.

syllabus_topics: Introduction to Elasticity and Strength of Materials.
Purpose of Elasticity and Strength of Materials.
Theoretical model of solid used in Strength of Materials. Mechanical prism.
Forces derived from the action of a system of forces on a mechanical prism.
Intrinsic components of the stress vector.
Study of stress vectors at a point. Stress matrix.
Necessary conditions between the elements of the stress matrix. Internal equilibrium and boundary equilibrium equations.
Deformation matrix and rotation matrix. Unit deformation vector.
Experimental relationship between stress and deformation. Tensile-compression test.
Laboratory Practice 1: Extensometry, calculation of Elastic modulus and Poisson's ratio using the experimental technique of extensometry.
General formulation of the elastic problem.

Computer Practice 1: General formulation of the elastic problem. Using specific software, the concepts of displacement, deformation, stress will be applied through their graphical representation and their interpretation will be explained.
Computer Practice 2: Calculation of forces using specific software.
Particular case: straight bar subjected to its own weight.
Elementary theory of torsion in prisms of circular cross-section.
Determination of torsional moments. Calculation of power transmission shafts.
Computer Practice 3: Calculation of stresses and deformations in a bar subjected to tensile and torsional loads.
Stresses produced in Simple Bending by Shear Force. Colignon's Theorem.

Laboratory Practice 2: Determination of deflection and rotation in bending. A simply supported aluminum tubular bar is subjected to bending using weights. Students will calculate, using Strength of Materials, the value of rotation and vertical displacement of certain sections and compare them with experimental values.
Computer Practice 4: Calculation of forces, rotations, and displacements in isostatic simple bending.
Stability of elastic equilibrium. Notion of critical load.
Value of the critical load according to the type of bar support. Buckling length.
Limits of application of Euler's Formula.
Laboratory Practice 3: Buckling of slender rectangular cross-section bars.

assessment_methods.method: Final theoretical/practical exam and/or cumulative/eliminatory partial exams

assessment_rules: The final grade (NA) is calculated as 0.80 times the exam grade (NE) plus 0.20 times the practical grade (NP). The exam grade (NE) is composed of Part I (30%) and Part II (70%). To pass the course, both Part I and Part II grades must be equal to or greater than 4.0 out of 10.0; otherwise, the final grade cannot exceed 4.0. A partial exam for Part I can waive that part in the final exam if the score is 5.0 or higher. Approved parts (P1 or P2) are retained for the extraordinary (July) resit of the same academic year, but not for subsequent years. The practical grade (NP) is not recoverable in the extraordinary call. For the global evaluation (resit), a final global theoretical/practical exam (EFG) and a global practical exam (EPG) are conducted; if EFG and EPG are both >=4, the final grade NF = 0.8 * EFG + 0.2 * EPG, otherwise NF = min(calculated NF, 4).
